# Thermal-to-Electric Ceiling for a 565 °C Molten-Salt Rankine Power Block

## 1. Why the naive Carnot number overstates the real ceiling

The textbook Carnot efficiency,

η_Carnot = 1 − T_cold/T_hot,

assumes the *source* is an isothermal reservoir at a single temperature T_hot. That is not what a molten-salt tower actually offers the power block. The hot tank sits at 565 °C (838 K), but as the salt flows through the steam generator train it gives up heat **sensibly** — cooling continuously from 565 °C down to the cold-tank return temperature of ~290 °C (563 K). The salt is a *finite-capacity, temperature-gliding* heat source, not an infinite isothermal bath at 838 K.

Treating it as isothermal at 838 K credits the cycle with being able to extract every joule of heat at the full 565 °C Carnot factor. In reality, only the first increment of heat is delivered at 565 °C; by the time the salt has cooled to 290 °C, the local Carnot factor available is much lower (at 563 K vs. a 313 K sink, the local factor is only ~44%, versus ~63% at 838 K). Averaging the *correct* local factor over the whole glide — weighted by how much heat is actually delivered at each temperature — necessarily gives a lower number than simply plugging the peak temperature into the Carnot formula.

So: **naive Carnot = upper bound on a single infinitesimal slice of the heat delivery, not on the whole process.** It is a real overstatement, not just a simplification, and we quantify the overstatement below.

## 2. The correct law-permitted ceiling: exergy-integrated (Lorenz-type) efficiency

**Ground truths used:**
- T_h = 565 °C = 838.15 K (hot tank)
- T_c = 290 °C = 563.15 K (cold tank — the salt is *not* cooled further; this is a design floor, not a sink)
- T_0 = heat-rejection sink temperature (313.15 K wet-cooled / ~323–333 K desert air-cooled)

**Derivation.** For a reversible engine drawing heat from a stream whose temperature falls continuously from T_h to T_c while rejecting waste heat to ambient T_0, consider an infinitesimal slice of heat δQ = c_p·dT given up while the salt is at local temperature T. The maximum work extractable from that slice (a local Carnot engine operating between T and T_0) is

δW = δQ·(1 − T_0/T)

Integrating from T_c to T_h:

W_max = ∫_{T_c}^{T_h} c_p(1 − T_0/T) dT = c_p[(T_h − T_c) − T_0·ln(T_h/T_c)]

Total heat delivered: Q = c_p(T_h − T_c)

**The specific heat c_p cancels**, leaving a clean closed-form ceiling that depends only on the three temperatures:

**η_ceiling = 1 − T_0·ln(T_h/T_c) / (T_h − T_c)**

This is the standard reversible-cycle (Lorenz) efficiency for a sensible-heat source with a glide — it is the correct "no law-of-thermodynamics-violated" ceiling for this architecture, strictly tighter than naive Carnot.

**Arithmetic** (T_h = 838.15 K, T_c = 563.15 K, so T_h/T_c = 1.4885, ln = 0.3976, T_h−T_c = 275 K):

| Sink T_0 | Naive Carnot (1−T₀/T_h) | Glide-corrected ceiling | Overstatement |
|---|---|---|---|
| 313 K (40 °C, wet cooling) | 62.6% | **54.7%** | 7.9 pts |
| 323 K (50 °C, desert air) | 61.4% | **53.3%** | 8.1 pts |
| 333 K (60 °C, desert air, hot design point) | 60.3% | **51.9%** | 8.4 pts |

So the true law-permitted ceiling for this architecture is **~52–55%**, roughly 8 percentage points (≈13% relative) below what naive Carnot would suggest — and this correction has nothing to do with engineering quality; it's a consequence of the source being a cooling, finite-capacity stream rather than an isothermal bath.

## 3. Representative current-practice numbers (power block only)

Isolating just the steam Rankine power block (turbine-generator-condenser-feedwater train; excluding heliostat field, receiver, and piping/tank thermal losses), for a 565 °C-salt tower delivering live steam at ~540 °C, 120–165 bar, single reheat, with regenerative feedwater heating — the standard configuration used at Gemasolar/Crescent-Dunes-class plants:

- **Gross turbine-cycle efficiency** (gross electric output ÷ thermal energy into the steam generator): **≈ 41–42%**
- **Net power-block efficiency** (after feedwater/condensate pumps, salt circulation pumps serving the power block, cooling system parasitics): **≈ 37–38%**

These numbers are consistent with — and essentially a direct analog of — a conventional subcritical/mildly-supercritical coal or oil steam plant running the same 540 °C/120–165 bar/single-reheat steam conditions, which is expected since the steam side of the cycle doesn't "know" its heat came from salt rather than combustion. (These are literature-representative figures, not pulled from a specific cited source in this pass — treat them as order-of-confidence ±1–2 points.)

## 4. Apples-to-apples gap (single, consistent T_0)

Using T_0 = 313 K (wet-cooling reference) consistently on **both** sides, so the comparison isn't contaminated by mixing a wet-cooled ceiling against an air-cooled real plant or vice versa:

- Ceiling: 54.7%
- Current practice (net): 37.5% (midpoint of 37–38%)
- **Gap: 17.2 percentage points (≈31% relative shortfall from the ceiling)**

Using gross turbine-cycle efficiency instead of net (i.e., excluding power-block parasitics from the comparison): 54.7% − 41.5% = **13.2 points (≈24% relative)**.

Re-running the same consistent-T_0 check at T_0 = 333 K (a desert air-cooled plant compared against a desert air-cooled ceiling) gives 51.9% vs. ~35.5% net ≈ **16.4 points (≈32% relative)** — essentially the same gap. This confirms the ~17-point / ~31% gap is a real power-block/cycle-design result, not an artifact of which sink temperature you happened to pick.

## 5. Decomposing the gap by physical cause

**(a) Isothermal boiling plateau vs. sensible-heat glide mismatch — mostly structurally locked (steam-cycle-intrinsic).**
Water boils at a fixed temperature at a given pressure. A single-pressure steam generator therefore draws heat from the salt across its full 565→290 °C glide but delivers most of that heat to the water/steam side across a much narrower effective temperature band (preheat, then an isothermal evaporation plateau, then superheat). This is a genuine thermodynamic mismatch between source and working fluid, distinct from (and additional to) the glide effect already priced into the Lorenz ceiling itself — the ceiling in §2 represents what a *perfectly glide-matched* ideal cycle could do; an actual steam Rankine cycle cannot match a continuous temperature glide with an isothermal phase change, however well engineered. Reheat and multi-stage regenerative feedwater heating claw back part of this (they're precisely attempts to approximate glide-matching), but a residual mismatch loss is intrinsic to the choice of steam/water as the working fluid. **Estimated contribution: ~3–5 points, mostly unrecoverable without changing the bottoming cycle's working fluid/topology** (e.g., a cycle whose heat-addition temperature itself varies continuously, like supercritical/transcritical CO2, inherently glide-matches better).

**(b) Finite approach/pinch ΔT in the salt-to-steam heat exchangers — partially recoverable, with diminishing returns.**
Real heat exchangers need a finite temperature difference to transfer heat in a HX of economic size; typical pinch/approach values of 15–25 °C mean live steam comes out around 540 °C rather than the full 565 °C the salt actually offers. This directly lowers the top-end Carnot factor the real cycle can access. It's genuinely recoverable — bigger/better HX surface, closer pinch — but asymptotically bounded (zero ΔT requires infinite area/cost), so the realistic recovery is a few degrees, not the full 25 °C. **Estimated contribution: ~2–3 points, of which maybe 1–1.5 points realistically recoverable** with next-generation HX design before cost makes further gains uneconomic.

**(c) Real turbine/generator/pump/piping irreversibilities — the most genuinely recoverable category.**
Turbine isentropic efficiencies (~88–92% vs. ideal 100%), generator and mechanical losses (~1–2%), throttling/pressure-drop losses, condenser subcooling, and imperfect feedwater-heater approaches all cost real efficiency that has nothing to do with the source's glide. These are the same losses any conventional steam plant fights, and they respond directly to known engineering levers: higher live-steam temperature/pressure (pushing toward true supercritical conditions, ~565–600 °C / 250+ bar), double reheat, advanced turbine blading/seals, larger/more feedwater heater stages. **Estimated contribution: ~6–8 points, of which ~4–6 points are plausibly recoverable** — this is exactly the gap between today's 540 °C/single-reheat/37–38% plants and best-in-class supercritical coal-equivalent steam cycles at similar top temperatures, which reach net efficiencies in the mid-40s%.

**(d) Desert/water-constrained siting forcing a higher rejection temperature — excluded from the gap by construction, but a real separate penalty.**
Because §4 deliberately holds T_0 fixed on both sides of the comparison, this factor does **not** show up in the 17-point gap figure — it's a confound we controlled for, not a loss category. But it is a real, additional efficiency penalty borne by actual air-cooled desert plants relative to a wet-cooled reference: moving T_0 from 313 K to 333 K costs about 2.5–3 points off *both* the ceiling and real-world net efficiency (54.7%→51.9% ceiling; a roughly proportional ~2 point hit to net practice). This is "shared" between ceiling and practice, essentially unrecoverable given the siting constraint (water scarcity is the reason these plants are air-cooled in the first place), and should be tracked separately from the power-block design gap rather than folded into it.

## 6. Final numeric verdict

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Naive Carnot (T_h=838K, T_0=313K) | 62.6% *(overstates true ceiling by ~8 pts)* |
| **Law-permitted ceiling** (glide-corrected, Lorenz/exergy, T_0=313K) | **54.7%** |
| Current practice — gross turbine-cycle | ~41.5% |
| Current practice — **net power block** | **~37.5%** |
| **Gap (ceiling − net practice)** | **~17 percentage points (~31% relative)** |
| Gap due to (a) steam/water glide-mismatch (bottoming-cycle-intrinsic) | ~3–5 pts — **mostly unrecoverable without abandoning steam Rankine** |
| Gap due to (b) HX pinch ΔT capping live-steam T below 565°C | ~2–3 pts — **~1–1.5 pts recoverable** via better/larger HX |
| Gap due to (c) turbine/pump/generator real-component losses | ~6–8 pts — **~4–6 pts recoverable** via supercritical steam, double reheat, better turbine tech |
| Gap due to (d) desert air-cooling vs. wet-cooling sink temperature | separate ~2–3 pt penalty — **excluded from the 17-pt gap above by holding T_0 fixed; itself largely unrecoverable given water constraints** |

**Bottom line:** Of the ~17-point gap between the true thermodynamic ceiling (~55%) and current practice (~38% net), roughly **5–8 percentage points are plausibly closeable through better steam-cycle engineering alone** — pushing live steam closer to the full 565 °C salt temperature, adopting supercritical/double-reheat steam conditions, tightening HX pinch, and using higher-efficiency turbomachinery — which could realistically bring net power-block efficiency into the mid-40s%. The remaining **~9–12 points are structurally locked in by the fundamental mismatch between water's isothermal boiling plateau and a sliding-temperature sensible-heat source**, and fully closing that residual would require abandoning single-fluid steam Rankine for a bottoming architecture that can track a continuous temperature glide — e.g., a supercritical-CO2 Brayton topping/bottoming combination or a genuinely multi-pressure-level steam train approximating a Kalina-style glide match — rather than any amount of incremental steam-turbine engineering.
